title: Non-Finites: Infinitives, Gerunds & Participles
description: Learn non-finite verbs for Grade 7: infinitives, gerunds and participles, the gerund vs participle difference, and dangling participles — with bilingual notes, practice and tests.

topics.title: Infinitives & Gerunds
topics.concept:
The infinitive is to + base verb. It can work as:

  • a noun: To err is human. (subject)
  • an adjective: She has work to do. (describes 'work')
  • an adverb of purpose: He went to buy milk. (why he went)

(The 'bare infinitive' — without 'to' — follows modals and some verbs: You must go. Let him play.)

The gerund is the -ing form used as a noun:

  • Swimming is good exercise. (subject)
  • I enjoy painting. (object)
  • She is fond of singing. (after a preposition)

examples.problem: Infinitive or gerund? Reading improves the mind.
examples.solution: Gerund — 'Reading' is the -ing form used as the subject (a noun).

examples.problem: What does the infinitive do here: He stopped to rest.?
examples.solution: It is an adverb of purpose — it tells why he stopped (in order to rest).

recap: Infinitive (to + verb) acts as noun, adjective or adverb of purpose
Gerund (-ing) acts as a noun (subject, object, after a preposition)

topics.title: Participles & Dangling Participles
topics.concept:
A participle is a verb form used as an adjective.

  • Present participle (-ing): the running water, a crying baby.
  • Past participle (-ed/-en): a broken vase, a written note.

A participle phrase can open a sentence and describe the subject: Having finished her work, she left.

Gerund vs participle: both end in -ing, but a gerund is a noun and a participle is an adjective:

  • The swimming pool (participle – describes pool)
  • I like swimming (gerund – the activity, a noun)

Dangling participle — a common error where the participle does not clearly describe the subject:

  • ❌ Walking down the road, the tree fell. (the tree wasn't walking!)
  • ✓ Walking down the road, I saw the tree fall.

examples.problem: Gerund or participle? The barking dog scared me.
examples.solution: Participle — 'barking' describes the noun 'dog' (it acts as an adjective).

examples.problem: Fix the dangling participle: Running fast, the bus was missed.
examples.solution: Running fast, I missed the bus. — the subject 'I' must be the one running.

recap: Participle = verb form used as an adjective (-ing / -ed)
A dangling participle must clearly describe the subject

questions.q: 'Walking is healthy.' — 'Walking' is a:
'He has a letter to post.' — 'to post' is:
'The broken window' — 'broken' is a:
Choose: 'She is interested in ___.'
'He ran to catch the bus.' — 'to catch' shows:
'A smiling child' — 'smiling' is a:
Choose: 'I enjoy ___ to music.'
'To forgive is divine.' — 'To forgive' is:
questions.explanation: Subject = infinitive used as a noun.

questions.q: Which has a dangling participle?
options: Reading the news, I felt sad.
Reading the news, the report shocked me.
While reading the news, I felt sad.
I read the news and felt sad.

questions.q: Choose: 'He is fond of ___ stories.'
'They let him ___.' (bare infinitive)
'The frightened crowd ran.' — 'frightened' acts as:
Spot the error: 'I look forward to see you soon.'
questions.explanation: 'look forward to' is followed by a gerund: 'to seeing'.

questions.q: Choose the correct meaning: 'He stopped to smoke.'
options: He stopped the habit of smoking.
He paused in order to smoke.
questions.explanation: 'stop + to-infinitive' = pause in order to do something.

questions.q: Identify the dangling modifier: 'Turning the corner, a beautiful lake came into view.'
questions.explanation: The lake can't turn the corner; the participle has no proper subject.

questions.q: Choose: 'I regret ___ you that the trip is cancelled.'
questions.explanation: 'regret + to-infinitive' is used for breaking news now: 'regret to tell'.

questions.q: Which sentence correctly uses a gerund after a preposition?
Choose the correct form: 'The teacher made the students ___ the poem.'
Rearrange: 'finished / having / homework / his / he / out / went'
options: Having finished his homework, he went out.
He having finished went out his homework.
Finished having his homework, he went out.
He went out having his homework finished.
questions.explanation: 'Having finished his homework, he went out.' is correct.

questions.q: Choose: 'It's no use ___ about it now.'

outcomes: Define non-finite verbs and name the three kinds
Use the infinitive (to + verb) as noun, adjective and adverb
Use the gerund (-ing) as a noun
Tell a gerund apart from a present participle

intro.en: A finite verb changes with the subject and tense (he plays, they played). A non-finite verb does not — it stays in one form and behaves like a noun, adjective or adverb. The three non-finites are the infinitive (to play), the gerund (playing), and the participle (playing / played).
intro.hi: परिमित क्रिया (finite verb) कर्ता और काल के अनुसार बदलती है (he plays, they played)। अपरिमित क्रिया (non-finite verb) नहीं बदलती — यह एक ही रूप में रहकर संज्ञा, विशेषण या क्रिया-विशेषण की तरह काम करती है। तीन non-finites हैं: infinitive (to play), gerund (playing), और participle (playing / played)।

real_life.situation:
You describe your plans:

You: I love reading, so I went to buy a new novel. Walking home, I met a friend who was excited about it.
real_life.why: 'reading' is a gerund (noun – the thing I love), 'to buy' is an infinitive (showing purpose), and 'Walking home' is a participle phrase (describing how I met the friend). One sentence shows all three non-finites at work.

rule_box.formula: Gerund = -ing as a NOUN · Participle = -ing/-ed as an ADJECTIVE
rule_box.example: Swimming is fun (gerund). The swimming pool is open (participle).

quick_test.q: In 'I enjoy painting', the word 'painting' is a:
quick_test.explanation: It is the object of 'enjoy' — a noun, so it is a gerund.

common_mistakes.note: After the preposition 'to' here, use a gerund.
After a preposition, use the gerund (dancing).

common_mistakes.right: Walking home, I felt the rain start.
common_mistakes.note: The participle must describe the subject (I).

error_detection.correct: I look forward to meeting you.

error_detection.sentence: Running fast, the bus was missed by him.
error_detection.correct: Running fast, he missed the bus.

sentence_correction.correct: Being tired, she left the work undone.

sentence_correction.correct: I am used to walking daily.

rearrangement.jumbled: her / having / work / finished / she / left
rearrangement.answer: Having finished her work, she left.

reading.passage: Hoping to win the prize, Aman practised every day. He loved painting, and his goal was to enter the school exhibition. Encouraged by his teacher, he worked hard. On the final day, holding his finished painting, he felt proud. Winning was wonderful, but the joy of creating mattered more.

questions.q: Find an infinitive used to show purpose.
questions.answer: to win (Hoping to win the prize) — it shows why he practised.

questions.q: Find a gerund used as a subject.
questions.answer: Winning (Winning was wonderful) — the -ing form acting as a noun/subject.

questions.q: Identify a participle phrase describing Aman.
questions.answer: "Encouraged by his teacher" or "holding his finished painting" — participle phrases describing him.

speaking: She went to meet her friend.
Having finished dinner, we watched a film.
I am interested in learning music.

writing.prompt: Write five sentences using a gerund as a subject, an infinitive of purpose, a present participle, a past participle, and a participle phrase opener.
writing.example: Painting relaxes me. I went to buy brushes. The drying canvas smelled fresh. A finished picture hung on the wall. Smiling proudly, I showed it to Mum.

micro_quiz.explanation: It is the subject (a noun) → gerund.
After a preposition, use the gerund.

micro_quiz.q: 'He went to school to study.' — 'to study' shows:
micro_quiz.explanation: Infinitive of purpose — why he went.

micro_quiz.q: Which sentence has a dangling participle?
options: Walking home, I saw a deer.
Walking home, the deer appeared to me.
I saw a deer while walking home.
While I walked home, I saw a deer.
micro_quiz.explanation: The deer wasn't walking — the participle is dangling.

challenge.q: Identify the function: 'There is no use crying over spilt milk.'
challenge.explanation: 'crying' is a gerund (a noun after 'use of').

challenge.q: Fix the sentence: 'Having eaten lunch, the dishes were washed.'
options: Having eaten lunch, we washed the dishes.
Having eaten lunch, the dishes were washed by us.
The dishes having eaten lunch were washed.
challenge.explanation: The doer of 'having eaten' must be the subject ('we').

challenge.q: Choose the correct form: 'I remember ___ him last year.'
challenge.explanation: 'remember + gerund' = recall a past event ('meeting him').

english.mindmap:
NON-FINITES
                |
   +------------+------------+
   |            |            |
 INFINITIVE   GERUND     PARTICIPLE
 to + verb    -ing as    -ing/-ed as
 noun/adj/    a NOUN     ADJECTIVE
 adverb(why)  subj/obj/  present/past
 bare inf.    after prep dangling=error
revision: Non-finite verbs don't change with subject/tense
Infinitive (to + verb): noun, adjective, or adverb of purpose
Gerund (-ing): a noun (subject, object, after a preposition)
A dangling participle must clearly describe the subject
